• In Yugoslavia, following the death of communist leader <color=#3366CC>Josip Broz Tito</color> in May 1980, the trend of political reform of
the communist system occurred along with a trend towards ethnic nationalism and inter-ethnic hostility, especially
in Serbia, beginning with the 1986 Memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts followed by the
agenda of Serbian communist leader <color=#3366CC>Slobodan Milošević</color> who aggressively pushed for increased political influence
of Serbs in the late 1980s, condemning non-Serb Yugoslav politicians who challenged his agenda as being
enemies of Serbs.
• There was <color=#3366CC>continuing civil strife</color> in <color=#3366CC>Northern Ireland</color>, including the adoption of hunger strikes by Irish Republican
Army prisoners seeking the reintroduction of political status.
• <color=#3366CC>Mikhail Gorbachev</color> became leader of the Soviet Union in 1985, and initiated major reforms to the Soviet Union's
government through increasing the rights of expressing political dissent and opening elections to opposition
candidates (while maintaining legal dominance of the Communist Party). Gorbachev pursued negotiation with the
United States to decrease tensions and eventually end the <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color>.
• During the <color=#3366CC>Revolutions of 1989</color>, most of the communist governments in Eastern Europe collapsed. The <color=#3366CC>fall of the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Berlin Wall</color> in 1989 would be followed in 1990 by the <color=#3366CC>German reunification</color>.
• The United Kingdom was governed by the <color=#3366CC>Conservative Party</color> under Prime Minister <color=#3366CC>Margaret Thatcher</color>, the first
female leader of a Western country. Under her Premiership, the party introduced widespread economic reforms
including the <color=#3366CC>privatisation</color> of industries and the de-regulation of <color=#3366CC>stock markets</color> echoing similar reforms of <color=#3366CC>US</color>
<color=#3366CC>President</color> <color=#3366CC>Ronald Reagan</color>. She was also a staunch opponent of communism, earning her the nickname The Iron
Lady.
• Poor industrial relations marked the beginning of the decade; the <color=#3366CC>UK miners' strike (1984–85)</color> was a major
industrial action affecting the UK coal industry. The strike by the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM) was led by
Arthur Scargill, although some NUM members considered it to be unconstitutional and did not observe it. The <color=#3366CC>BBC</color>
has referred to the strike as "the most bitter industrial dispute in British history." At its height, the strike involved
142,000 mineworkers, making it the biggest since the 1926 General Strike.
• In November 1982, <color=#3366CC>Leonid Brezhnev</color>, who had led the Soviet Union since 1964, died. He was followed in quick
succession by <color=#3366CC>Yuri Andropov</color>, the former KGB chief, and Konstantin Chernenko, both of whom were in poor health
during their short tenures in office.
• Presidents of France were <color=#3366CC>Valéry Giscard d'Estaing</color> and <color=#3366CC>François Mitterrand</color>. The Chancellors of West Germany
were <color=#3366CC>Helmut Schmidt</color> and <color=#3366CC>Helmut Kohl</color>.
Asia
• The Prime Ministers of Japan were Masayoshi Ōhira, Zenkō Suzuki, <color=#3366CC>Yasuhiro Nakasone</color>, Noboru Takeshita,
Sōsuke Uno and Toshiki Kaifu.
• Following the assassination of Park Chung-hee, South Korean president <color=#3366CC>Chun Doo Hwan</color> came to power at the
end of 1979 and ruled as a dictator until his presidential term expired in 1987. He was responsible for the <color=#3366CC>Gwangju</color>
<color=#3366CC>Uprising</color> in May 1980 when police and soldiers battled armed protesters. Relations with North Korea showed little
sign of improvement during the 1980s. In 1983, when Chun was in Burma, a bomb apparently planted by North
Korean agents killed a number of South Korean government officials. The <color=#3366CC>June Democratic Struggle</color> in 1987, a
nationwide pro-democracy movement in South Korea, leads to democratic reforms, an end to authoritarian rule and
democratic elections. After leaving office, Chun was succeeded by Roh Tae Woo, the first democratic ruler of the
country, which saw its international prestige greatly rise with hosting the Olympics in 1988. Roh pursued a policy of
normalizing relations with China and the Soviet Union, but had to face militant left-wing student groups who
demanded reunification with North Korea and the withdrawal of US troops.
• In the Philippines, after 20 years of dictatorship, Philippine president <color=#3366CC>Ferdinand Marcos</color> was ousted from power,
fleeing with <color=#3366CC>Imelda Marcos</color> and their children to <color=#3366CC>Hawaii</color> and replaced by <color=#3366CC>Corazon Aquino</color> through the non-violent
<color=#3366CC>People Power Revolution</color> from 22 to 25 February 1986.
• Democratization in South Korea and Taiwan, having lasted 42 and 27 years under the authoritarian regime since
the end of World War II and the <color=#3366CC>Korean War</color> (including the lifting of martial law in Taiwan and the first direct
presidential elections in South Korea).
• The 1988 Summer Olympics were held in South Korea, the first time the country hosted them.
Africa
• A widespread <color=#3366CC>famine hit Ethiopia</color> from 1983 to 1985, affecting 7.75 million people, killing around 300,000 to 1.2
million. 400,000 refugees left the country. Blame for the famine has been attributed to drought, <color=#3366CC>Ethiopia's civil war</color>,
and policies taken by the <color=#3366CC>Derg</color> military regime.
Assassinations and attempts
Prominent assassinations, targeted killings, and assassination attempts include:
Disasters
Natural disasters
• <color=#3366CC>Mount St. Helens</color> erupted in <color=#3366CC>Washington</color>, US on 18 May 1980, killing 57 people.
• <color=#3366CC>HIV/AIDS</color>, a global pandemic that has killed over 40 million people, was identified in the 1980s, with the first
reported cases in 1981.
• On 17 October 1989, the Loma Prieta earthquake struck the San Francisco Bay Area during game three of the
1989 World Series, gaining worldwide attention. Sixty-five people were killed and thousands injured, with major
structural damage on freeways and buildings and broken gas-line fires in San Francisco, California. The cost of the
damage totaled US$13 billion (1989 US$).
• The 1988–89 North American drought decimated the US with many parts of the country affected. This was the
worst drought to hit the United States in many years. The drought caused $60 billion in damage (between $80
billion and $120 billion for 2008 US$). The concurrent <color=#3366CC>heat waves</color> killed 5,800 to 17,000 people in the United
States.
• Hurricane Allen (1980), Hurricane Alicia (1983), Hurricane Gilbert (1988), Hurricane Joan (1988), and Hurricane
Hugo (1989) were some notably destructive Atlantic hurricanes of the 1980s.
• Other <color=#3366CC>natural disasters</color> of the 1980s include the 1982–1983 El Niño which brought destructive weather to most of
the world; the 1985 Mexico City earthquake, which registered 8.0 on the <color=#3366CC>moment magnitude scale</color> and devastated
Mexico City and other areas throughout central Mexico; the 1985 Nevado del Ruiz <color=#3366CC>lahar</color> in <color=#3366CC>Colombia</color>; the 1986
Lake Nyos limnic eruption in <color=#3366CC>Cameroon</color>; and the 1988 Armenian earthquake, which rocked the <color=#3366CC>Caucasus</color> region of
the <color=#3366CC>USSR</color>.
Non-natural disasters
• In 1980, Dan-Air Flight 1008, a Boeing 727, crashed on approach to <color=#3366CC>Tenerife</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Canary Islands</color>, killing 146
people on board.
• In 1980, Saudia Flight 163, a Lockheed L-1011 TriStar, caught fire moments after takeoff from the <color=#3366CC>Saudi Arabian</color>
capital of <color=#3366CC>Riyadh</color>. The flight immediately returned to the airport, but evacuation of the plane was delayed and all
301 people aboard died.
• In 1982, Pan Am Flight 759, a Boeing 727, was forced down by microburst while on approach to New Orleans
International Airport, killing 153 people.
• In 1983, Korean Air Lines Flight 007, a <color=#3366CC>Boeing 747</color> carrying 269 people between New York City and <color=#3366CC>Seoul</color> via
<color=#3366CC>Anchorage</color>, was shot down by Soviet fighter jets after accidentally straying into Soviet prohibited airspace, killing
everyone on board.
• In 1984, the <color=#3366CC>Bhopal disaster</color> resulted from a toxic methyl isocyanate (MIC) gas leak at the Union Carbide plant in
<color=#3366CC>Bhopal, India</color>, killing 3,000 immediately and ultimately claiming 15,000–20,000 lives.
• In 1985, the Heysel Stadium disaster occurred before the European Cup final in <color=#3366CC>Brussels</color>, Belgium, when a crowd
crush led to 39 deaths and 600 injuries.
• In 1985, Air India Flight 182, a Boeing 747 flying from <color=#3366CC>Montreal</color> to <color=#3366CC>Bombay</color> via London and Delhi, is blown up over
Irish waters by a bomb planted by <color=#3366CC>Sikh separatists</color>, killing all 320 passengers and crew on board. This was the
deadliest act of aviation terrorism until the <color=#3366CC>September 11 attacks</color> of 2001.
• In 1985, Delta Air Lines Flight 191, a Lockheed L-1011 TriStar, crashed on approach to Dallas/Fort Worth
International Airport in <color=#3366CC>Texas</color> due to a microburst. 137 people were killed while 27 survived.
• Japan Air Lines Flight 123, a Boeing 747 carrying 524 people, crashed in 1985, while on a flight from Tokyo to
<color=#3366CC>Osaka</color>, killing 520 of the people on board, leaving four survivors. This was the deadliest single-aircraft crash to
date.
• In 1985, Arrow Air Flight 1285R, a Douglas DC-8, stalled and crashed seconds after taking off from Gander,
Newfoundland. All 256 people on board, many of them US servicemen returning home from duty overseas,
perished.
• In 1986, the NASA Space Shuttle Challenger <color=#3366CC>disintegrated</color> 73 seconds after launch, killing all of the crew on board.
This was the first disaster involving the destruction of a NASA Space Shuttle. A faulty O-ring was the cause of the
accident.
• On 26 April 1986, the <color=#3366CC>Chernobyl disaster</color>, a large-scale <color=#3366CC>nuclear meltdown</color> in the Ukrainian SSR, Soviet Union,
spread a large amount of radioactive material across Europe, killing 47 people, dooming countless others to future
radiation-related cancer, and causing the displacement of 300,000 people.
• In 1986, Aeroméxico Flight 498, a <color=#3366CC>Douglas DC-9</color>, crashed after colliding with a private Piper Cherokee over
Cerritos, California, killing 64 on both aircraft and 15 others on the ground. On the same day, the Soviet passenger
ship Admiral Nakhimov sank after colliding with the bulk carrier Pyotr Vasev in the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color>, killing 423 people.
• In 1987, LOT Flight 5055, an Ilyushin Il-62M caught fire due to an uncontained engine failure and subsequently
crashed, killing all 183 passengers and crew.
• In 1987, Northwest Airlines Flight 255, a McDonnell Douglas MD-82, crashed almost immediately after takeoff
Detroit Wayne Airport in <color=#3366CC>Michigan</color> due to pilot error, killing 156 on board.
• In 1987, a fire broke out on South African Airways Flight 295, a Boeing 747, eventually causing the aircraft to crash
into the Indian Ocean. All 159 aboard were killed.
• On 20 December 1987, the <color=#3366CC>Philippine</color> passenger ferry MV Doña Paz burned and sank after colliding with the oil
tanker MT Vector off the island of <color=#3366CC>Marinduque</color>. With an estimated death toll of over 4,000, this was and remains the
world's deadliest peacetime maritime disaster.
• In 1988, Iran Air Flight 655, an <color=#3366CC>Airbus A300</color> en route from Tehran to <color=#3366CC>Dubai</color> via <color=#3366CC>Bandar Abbas</color>, was shot down by
the US missile cruiser over the <color=#3366CC>Strait of Hormuz</color>, killing all 290 people on the plane. The event is one of the most
controversial aviation occurrences of all time, with the true cause disputed between the Americans and the
Iranians.
• In 1988, <color=#3366CC>Pan Am Flight 103</color>, a Boeing 747 en route from Frankfurt to Detroit (via London and New York), was
destroyed by a bomb while it was flying over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing the 259 passengers and crew members on
board and 11 people on the ground. This was the worst terrorist attack to have occurred on British soil.
• On 24 March 1989, the <color=#3366CC>oil tanker</color> Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef in <color=#3366CC>Alaska</color>'s Prince William Sound
spilling an estimated equivalent of 260,000 to 750,000 barrels of crude oil. Although not among the largest oil spills
in history, its remote and sensitive location made it one of the most devastating ecological disasters, with
after-effects continuing to be felt present-day.
• In 1989, the Hillsborough disaster occurs during a FA Cup semi-final in <color=#3366CC>Sheffield</color>, England, fatally crushing 96
football fans and injuring nearly 1,000 more.
• In 1989, United Airlines Flight 232, a McDonnell Douglas DC-10 carrying 296 people, suffered an in-flight engine
failure and was forced to crash-land at Sioux City, Iowa. 185 survived, while 111 were killed when the plane burst
into flames upon touchdown.
Science and technology
Medicine and biology
The 1980s had many fundamental advances in medicine and biology. The first <color=#3366CC>surrogate pregnancy</color> of an unrelated
child took place on 13 April 1986, in Michigan. The first <color=#3366CC>genetically modified</color> crops, <color=#3366CC>tobacco</color> (Nicotiana) plants were
grown in China in 1988.
<color=#3366CC>Gene therapy</color> techniques became established by the end of the 1980s, allowing gene tagging and <color=#3366CC>gene therapy</color> to
become a possibility, both of which were first performed in human beings in May 1989 and September 1990,
respectively.
Electronics and computers
<color=#3366CC>Arcade</color> and video games had been growing in popularity since the late 1970s, and by 1982 were a major industry. In
the United States, a variety of factors, including a glut of low-quality games and the rise of home computers, caused a
<color=#3366CC>tremendous crash</color> in late 1983. For the next three years, the video game market practically ceased to exist in the US.
But in the second half of the decade, it would be revived by <color=#3366CC>Nintendo</color>, whose Famicom console and mascot <color=#3366CC>Mario</color> had
been enjoying considerable success in Japan, which did not have an equivalent crash, since 1983. Renamed the
<color=#3366CC>Nintendo Entertainment System</color> (NES), it would claim 90% of the American video game market by 1989. The 1980s
are considered to be the decade when video games achieved massive popularity. In 1980, Pac-Man was introduced to
arcades, and became one of the most popular video games of all time. Also in 1980, Game & Watch was created; it
was not one of the best known game systems, but it facilitated mini-games and was concurrent with the NES. <color=#3366CC>Donkey</color>
<color=#3366CC>Kong</color>, released in 1981, was a smash arcade hit and market breakthrough for <color=#3366CC>Nintendo</color>. <color=#3366CC>Super Mario Bros.</color>, Duck Hunt,
<color=#3366CC>Dragon Quest</color>, <color=#3366CC>The Legend of Zelda</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Mega Man</color> series would become major hits for the console.
The <color=#3366CC>personal computer</color> experienced explosive growth in the 1980s, transitioning from a hobbyist's toy to a full-fledged
consumer product. The IBM PC, launched in 1981, became the dominant computer for professional users. Commodore
created the most popular home computers of both 8-bit and 16-bit generations. MSX standard was the dominant
computer platform in Japan and in most parts of Asia. <color=#3366CC>Apple Computer</color> superseded its <color=#3366CC>Apple II</color> and Lisa models by
introducing the first Macintosh computer in 1984. It was the first commercially successful personal computer to use a
<color=#3366CC>graphical user interface</color> (GUI) and <color=#3366CC>mouse</color>, which started to become general features in computers after the middle of
the decade. Electronics and computers were also at the forefront of the advertising industry, with many commercials
like "1984" from Apple achieving acclaim and pop-culture relevance.
<color=#3366CC>Walkman</color> and boomboxes, invented during the late 1970s, became very popular as they were introduced to various
countries in the early 1980s, and had a profound impact on the music industry and youth culture. Consumer <color=#3366CC>VCRs</color> and
video rental stores became commonplace as <color=#3366CC>VHS</color> won out over the competing Betamax standard. In addition, in the
early 1980s various companies began selling compact, modestly priced <color=#3366CC>synthesizers</color> to the public. This, along with the
development of <color=#3366CC>Musical Instrument Digital Interface</color> (MIDI), made it easier to integrate and synchronize synthesizers
and other electronic instruments, like drum machines, for use in musical composition.
<color=#3366CC>High definition television</color> (HDTV) of both the analog and digital variety were first developed in the 1980s though their
use did not become widespread until the mid-2000s.
In 1981, Hayes Microcomputer Products started selling the Smartmodem. The Smartmodem paved the way for the
modern modems that exist today, mainly because it was the first modem to transform what had previously required a
two-stage process into a process involving only one stage. The Smartmodem contributed to the rise in popularity of
<color=#3366CC>BBS</color> systems in the 1980s and early 1990s, which were the main way to connect to remote computers and perform
various social and entertainment activities before the <color=#3366CC>Internet</color> and the <color=#3366CC>World Wide Web</color> finally became popular in the
mid-1990s.
The 1980s witnessed a rapid expansion in the communications industry. Almost a decade after <color=#3366CC>Martin Cooper</color>, then an
employee of Motorola, made the first mobile phone call in 1973, Millicom Inc., a telecommunications agency, and E.F.
Johnson & Co., introduced the first portable cellular phone commercially available for use on a cellular network, the
"Lunch Box" in 1981. Two years later, Motorola launched the DynaTAC 8000X or the "Brick," the first commercially
available handheld mobile phone weighing 3 pounds (1.4 kg). While revolutionary, these early products were bulky and
challenging to handle. This led to fierce competition in the market, with companies vying to produce a lighter, more
portable phone, setting the stage for the future of mobile technology.
The race for a slimmer version of the portable cell phone was underway, and technology entrepreneur Jan Stenbeck
was determined to lead the charge. Stenbeck founded the tech start-up Technophone with a singular goal in mind: to
create a lightweight, pocket-sized mobile phone. In 1986, under the guidance of Technophones <color=#3366CC>chief executive officer</color>,
Nils Martensson, the company unveiled the first pocket-sized mobile phone, the Excell PCT105.
Information technology
• During the decade <color=#3366CC>Microsoft</color> released the operating systems <color=#3366CC>MS-DOS</color> (1981), Windows 1.0 (1985), and Windows
• Mathematical Software MathLab, introduced in 1988, by Stephen Wolfram.
• The <color=#3366CC>CD</color> – the most basic CD ("Digital Audio Compact Disc") was released in October 1982 for distribution and
listening to digital audio, and at the time contained up to 74 minutes of music.
• <color=#3366CC>TCP/IP</color>: <color=#3366CC>ARPANET</color> officially changed its main protocol from NCP to <color=#3366CC>TCP/IP</color> on 1 January 1983, when the new
protocols were activated. The TCP/IP protocol will become the dominant communications protocol from then
onwards, and would be used as the foundation on which the <color=#3366CC>Internet</color> would be based.
• The <color=#3366CC>GNU Project</color> (1983). The <color=#3366CC>Free Software Foundation</color> (1985).
• FidoNet – In 1984, FidoNet was launched, enabling <color=#3366CC>BBS</color> users to send private messages (e-mails) and public
messages (in the forum) between all BBS systems that were connected to the FidoNet network, in addition to
sending files to each other. The rise in popularity and availability of the Internet around the world around the
mid-1990s eventually contributed to the irrelevance of FidoNet.
• <color=#3366CC>World Wide Web</color> – In 1989, the British computer scientist <color=#3366CC>Tim Berners-Lee</color> first proposed a project to his employer
<color=#3366CC>CERN</color>, based on the concept of hypertext, to facilitate sharing and updating information among researchers. In
mid-November 1989 he would develop the first successful communication between a <color=#3366CC>Hypertext Transfer Protocol</color>
(HTTP) client and server via the <color=#3366CC>internet</color>. In the coming years Berners-Lee developed the system which would later
become the foundation of the <color=#3366CC>World Wide Web</color>.
Space exploration
American interplanetary probes continued in the 1980s, the Voyager duo being the most known. After making a flyby of
Jupiter in 1979, they went near Saturn in 1980–1981. <color=#3366CC>Voyager 2</color> reached Uranus in 1986 (just a few days before the
Challenger disaster), and Neptune in 1989 before the probes exited the Solar System.
No American probes were launched to Mars in the 1980s, and the Viking probes, launched there in 1975, completed
their operations by 1982. The Soviets launched two Mars probes in 1988, but they failed.
The arrival of <color=#3366CC>Halley's Comet</color> in 1986 was met by a series of Soviet, Japanese and <color=#3366CC>European Space Agency</color> (ESA)
probes, namely Halley Armada.
After a six-year hiatus, American space flights with astronauts resumed with the launch of the Space Shuttle Columbia
in April 1981. The shuttle program progressed smoothly from there, with three more orbiters entering service in
1983–1985. But that all came to an end with the <color=#3366CC>tragic loss</color> of the Challenger (STS-51-L) on 28 January 1986, taking
with it seven astronauts, including <color=#3366CC>Christa McAuliffe</color>, who was to have been the first teacher in space. In full view of the
world, a faulty O-ring on the right solid rocket booster allowed hot gases to burn through the external fuel tank and
cause it to explode, destroying the shuttle in the process. Extensive efforts were made to improve <color=#3366CC>NASA</color>'s increasingly
careless management practices, and to make the shuttle safer. Flights resumed with the launch of Discovery in
September 1988.
The Soviet program with cosmonauts went well during the decade, experiencing only minor setbacks. The Salyut 6
space station, launched in 1977, was replaced by Salyut 7 in 1982. Then came <color=#3366CC>Mir</color> in 1986, which ended up operating
for more than a decade, and was destined to be the last in the line of Soviet space stations that had begun in 1971.
One of the Soviet Union's last "superprojects" was the Buran space shuttle; it was only used once, in 1988.
Automobiles
The American auto industry began in the 1980s in a thoroughly grim situation, faced with poor quality control, rising
import competition, and a severe economic downturn. <color=#3366CC>Chrysler</color> and American Motors (AMC) were near bankruptcy, and
Ford was little better off. Only <color=#3366CC>General Motors</color> (GM) continued with business as usual. But the auto makers recovered
with the economy by 1983, and in 1985 auto sales in the United States hit a new record. However, the Japanese were
now a major presence, and would begin manufacturing cars in the US to get around tariffs. In 1986, Hyundai became
the first Korean auto maker to enter the American market. In the same year, the Yugoslavian-built Yugo was brought to
the US, but the car was so small and cheap, that it became the subject of jokes. It was sold up to 1991, when economic
sanctions against Yugoslavia forced its withdrawal from the American market.
As the decade progressed, cars became smaller and more efficient in design. In 1983, <color=#3366CC>Ford</color> design teams began to
incorporate aerodynamic styling to decrease drag while in motion. The Thunderbird was one of the first cars to receive
these design changes. In 1985, Ford released the Taurus with a design that was revolutionary among domestic mass
market automobiles.
GM began suffering significant losses in the late 1980s, partially the result of chairman Roger Smith's restructuring
attempts, and partially because of increasingly dated cars. An example were customers who increasingly purchased
European luxury cars rather than Cadillacs. In 1985, GM started Saturn (the first new American make since the Edsel),
with the goal of producing high-quality import fighters. Production would not begin until 1990.
Chrysler introduced its new compact, front-wheel drive K-cars in 1981. Under the leadership of <color=#3366CC>Lee Iacocca</color>, the
company turned a profit again the following year, and by 1983 paid off its government loans. A succession of models
using this automobile platform followed. The most significant were the <color=#3366CC>minivans</color> in 1984. These proved a to be popular
and they would dominate the van market for more than a decade. In 1987, Chrysler purchased the Italian makes of
Lamborghini and Maserati. In the same year, Chrysler bought AMC from <color=#3366CC>Renault</color> laying to rest the last significant
independent US automaker, but acquiring the hugely profitable Jeep line and continuing the Eagle brand until the late
The DMC DeLorean was the brainchild of <color=#3366CC>John DeLorean</color>, a flamboyant former GM executive. Production of the
gull-winged sports car began in Northern Ireland in 1981. John DeLorean was arrested in October 1982 in a sting
operation where he was attempting to sell cocaine to save his struggling company. He was acquitted of all charges in
1984, but too late for the DeLorean Motor Company, which closed down in 1983. The DeLorean gained renewed fame
afterward as the time machine in the Back to the Future film trilogy.
The imposition of corporate average fuel economy (CAFE) fuel-mileage standards in 1979 spelled the end of big-block
engines, but performance cars and <color=#3366CC>convertibles</color> reemerged in the 1980s. Turbochargers were widely used to boost the
performance of small cars, and technology from fuel injection began to take over from the widely used application of
carburetors by the late 1980s. Front-wheel drive also became dominant.
The 1980s marked the decline of European brands in North America by the end of the decade. Renault, <color=#3366CC>Citroën</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>Peugeot</color> ceased importation by the end of the decade. Alfa Romeo would continue until 1993. <color=#3366CC>Fiat</color> also ceased imports
to North America in the 1980s.
Economics
• The early 1980s was marked by a severe global economic recession that affected much of the developed world.
• Inflation peaked in the US in April 1980 at 14.76% and subsequently fell to a low of 1.10% in December 1986 but
then rebounded to 4.65% at the end of the decade.
• Finland's economy grew by almost the fastest pace in the world, which eventually culminated in the recession of
the 1990s Finnish economy. In Finland, the 1980s were called the "Nousukausi", or "economic upswing".
• In the late 1980s, Japan experienced an economic bubble, which would culminate in a stock market crash in 1991
that would begin a <color=#3366CC>period of economic stagnation</color>.
• Developing countries reliant on loans from the <color=#3366CC>International Monetary Fund</color> would experience debt crises
throughout the 1980s.
• <color=#3366CC>Laissez faire</color> and <color=#3366CC>neoliberal</color> economics have a resurgence in the developed world, led by the UK and US which
emphasised reduced government intervention, lower taxes and deregulation of the stock markets, measures that
became associated with an economic revival in the mid- to late-1980s.
• Brazil and Mexico suffers from a debt crisis in Latin America starting in 1982 under President <color=#3366CC>João Figueiredo</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Miguel de la Madrid</color>. Economic problems worsened between 1979 and 1985 by firing and resignation of most
officials of the Brazilian and Mexican government after the Diretas Já movement in 1984, and a failed response of
emergency aid in the Mexico City earthquake just after the 175th anniversary of independence holiday in 1985.
Tancredo Neves (later succeeded by <color=#3366CC>José Sarney</color> three months later) won a direct presidential election in 1985,
marking the end of a <color=#3366CC>21-year military dictatorship</color>, while Mexico's <color=#3366CC>Carlos Salinas de Gortari</color> won a controversial
presidential election in 1988 amid charges of voter fraud, bribery, corruption and other abuses of power.
• Enactment of the Canada–United States Free Trade Agreement in 1989 to further establish a strong economic
bond between the two prosperous neighbor countries of North America.
• In the Soviet Union, the eleventh Five-Year Plan was initiated in 1981 during a period of economic stagnation that
began in the late 1970s. The Plan was a near failure, as most of the targets were not met. With the ascent of
<color=#3366CC>Mikhail Gorbachev</color> as General Secretary of the <color=#3366CC>Communist Party</color>, the twelfth Five-Year Plan sought to accelerate
and <color=#3366CC>restructure</color> the Soviet economy through reforms to decentralize production and distribution systems.
• Under the leadership of <color=#3366CC>Deng Xiaoping</color>, China embarked on the <color=#3366CC>reform and opening up</color> in the 1980s, opening the
country's economy to the West and allowing capitalist enterprises to operate in a <color=#3366CC>market socialist system</color>. The
corruption of <color=#3366CC>Communist Party</color> leadership was met by dissent from students and workers in the <color=#3366CC>Tiananmen Square</color>
<color=#3366CC>protests of 1989</color> which were suppressed by the <color=#3366CC>People's Liberation Army</color>.
• The <color=#3366CC>Solidarity movement</color> began in Poland in 1980, involving workers demanding political liberalization and
democracy in Poland. Attempts by the Communist government to prevent the rise of the Solidarity movement failed
and negotiations between the movement and the government took place. Solidarity would be instrumental in
encouraging people in other communist states to demand political reform.
• The financial world and the stock market were glamorized in a way they had not been since the 1920s, and figures
like <color=#3366CC>Donald Trump</color> and <color=#3366CC>Michael Milken</color> were widely seen as symbols of the decade. Widespread fear of Japanese
economic strength would grip the United States in the 1980s.
• The "Black Monday" <color=#3366CC>stock market crash</color> on 19 October 1987, decreased the value of the Dow Jones Industrial
Average by more than 22%, causing widespread secondary drops in world markets.
• During the 1980s, for the first time in world history, transpacific trade (with <color=#3366CC>East Asia</color>, such as China, and Latin
America, primarily with Mexico) equaled that of transatlantic trade (with <color=#3366CC>Western Europe</color> or with neighboring
Canada), solidifying American economic power.
• The Savings and Loan crisis and Keating five scandal.
• The phrase Big Bang, used in reference to the sudden deregulation of financial markets, was coined to describe
measures, including abolition of fixed commission charges and of the distinction between stockjobbers and
stockbrokers on the London Stock Exchange and change from open-outcry to electronic, screen-based trading,
effected by Margaret Thatcher in 1986.
Popular culture
Music
In the United States, <color=#3366CC>MTV</color> was launched and <color=#3366CC>music videos</color> began to have a larger effect on the record industry. Pop

artists/bands such as <color=#3366CC>Duran Duran</color>, <color=#3366CC>Michael Jackson</color>, <color=#3366CC>George Michael</color>, <color=#3366CC>Whitney Houston</color>, <color=#3366CC>Prince</color>, <color=#3366CC>Cyndi Lauper</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Madonna</color> mastered the format and helped turn this new product into a profitable business. At the beginning of the
decade <color=#3366CC>new wave</color> fell from favor with the rise of the New Romantic, new pop and <color=#3366CC>synthpop</color> genres developed by many
British and American artists, popular phenomena throughout the decade especially in the early and mid-1980s. Music
evolved into fragmented and combined subgenres, including house, goth, and rap metal. Famous music videos include
those of <color=#3366CC>Peter Gabriel</color>.
The advent of numerous new technologies had a significant impact on 1980s music, and led to a distinct production
aesthetic that included <color=#3366CC>synthesizer</color> sounds, <color=#3366CC>drum machines</color> and drum reverb.
<color=#3366CC>Duran Duran</color>, the biggest band of the 1980s, were leaders in the Second British Invasion, with a level of fame similar to
Beatlemania by 1985. Their debut single was "Planet Earth" (1981). Their breakthrough album was Rio (1982). The
single "Hungry Like the Wolf" was number 1 in Canada. UK number 1 singles include "Is There Something I Should
Know?" and "The Reflex", which was the band's most successful single and was also number 1 in the US and on the
Eurochart Hot 100. "A View to a Kill", theme song of the James Bond film, was number 1 in the US. "Notorious" was
number 1 in Italy, Spain and Canada. "The Wild Boys" was number 1 in West Germany and South Africa. The band
went on to sell over 100 million records and win Brit, Grammy and MTV awards.
<color=#3366CC>Michael Jackson</color> was one of the icons of the 1980s and his <color=#3366CC>leather jacket</color>, white <color=#3366CC>glove</color>, and Moonwalk dance were often
imitated. Jackson's 1982 album <color=#3366CC>Thriller</color> became—and currently remains—the best-selling album of all time, with sales
estimated by various sources as somewhere between 65 and 110 million copies worldwide. His 1987 album <color=#3366CC>Bad</color> sold
over 45 million copies and became the first album to have five number-one singles chart on the Billboard Hot 100.
Jackson had the most number-one singles throughout the decade (9), and spent the most weeks at number one (27
weeks). His 1987 Bad World Tour grossed over $125 million worldwide, making it the highest grossing world tour by a
solo artist during the decade. Jackson earned numerous awards and titles during the 1980s, the most notable of which
were a record eight <color=#3366CC>Grammy Awards</color> and eight American Music Awards in 1984, and the honor of "Artist of the Decade"
by US President <color=#3366CC>George H. W. Bush</color>. Jackson was arguably the biggest star during this time, and would eventually sell
more than one billion records around the world.
<color=#3366CC>Prince</color> was a popular star of the 1980s and the most successful chart act of the decade. His breakthrough album 1999,
released in 1982, produced three top-ten hits and the album itself charted at number nine on the Billboard 200. His
sixth studio album <color=#3366CC>Purple Rain</color> was an international success, boosting Prince to superstardom and selling over 25
million copies worldwide. The album produced the US number-one singles, "When Doves Cry" and "Let's Go Crazy"
and sold 13 million copies in the US as of 1996. Prince released an album every year for the rest of the decade, all
charting within the top ten, with the exception of Lovesexy. He went on to sell over 120 million records worldwide and
win seven <color=#3366CC>Grammy Awards</color>.
The '80s were above all a time of international corporatization... [<color=#3366CC>Rock music</color>] was reconceived as <color=#3366CC>intellectual property</color>,
as a form of <color=#3366CC>capital</color> itself... The '80s were when stars replaced artists as bearers of significance... The '80s took rock
sexuality and rock sexism over the top... The '80s were a time of renewed racial turmoil after ten-plus years of polite
resegregation... Technology changed everything in the '80s. <color=#3366CC>Cable</color> brought us <color=#3366CC>MTV</color> and the triumph of the image.
<color=#3366CC>Synthesizers</color> inflected the sounds that remained. <color=#3366CC>Sampling</color> revolutionized rock and roll's proprietary relationship to its
own history. <color=#3366CC>Cassettes</color> made private music portable—and public. <color=#3366CC>Compact discs</color> inflated profitability as they faded into
the background of busy lives.

<color=#3366CC>Madonna</color> and <color=#3366CC>Whitney Houston</color> were groundbreaking female artists of the decade. The <color=#3366CC>keyboard synthesizer</color> and <color=#3366CC>drum</color>
<color=#3366CC>machine</color> were among the most popular instruments in music during the 1980s. After the 1980s, electronic instruments
continued to be the main component of mainstream pop.
Synth pop and new pop musicians included the Eurythmics, <color=#3366CC>Pet Shop Boys</color>, Spandau Ballet, A Flock of Seagulls,
INXS, Ultravox, Men Without Hats, Icehouse, Toni Basil, OMD, Visage, Alphaville, <color=#3366CC>A-ha</color>, Martha and the Muffins, Talk
Talk and <color=#3366CC>Depeche Mode</color>. Pop rock bands included Tears for Fears and Transvision Vamp. Ska bands included
Madness and <color=#3366CC>The Specials</color>.
Stock Aitken Waterman songs were sung by Bananarama, Dead or Alive, <color=#3366CC>Rick Astley</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kylie Minogue</color> and <color=#3366CC>Donna</color>
<color=#3366CC>Summer</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Hard rock</color>, <color=#3366CC>heavy metal</color>, and <color=#3366CC>glam metal</color> became some of the most dominant music genres of the decade, peaking with

the arrival of such bands as <color=#3366CC>Mötley Crüe</color>, <color=#3366CC>Guns N' Roses</color>, <color=#3366CC>Metallica</color>, <color=#3366CC>Iron Maiden</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bon Jovi</color>, <color=#3366CC>Def Leppard</color>, Poison,
Europe, <color=#3366CC>Megadeth</color>, <color=#3366CC>Slayer</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sepultura</color>, Anthrax, and virtuoso guitarists such as Joe Satriani and Yngwie Malmsteen.
The scene also helped 1970s hard rock artists and bands such as <color=#3366CC>AC/DC</color>, Heart, <color=#3366CC>Ozzy Osbourne</color>, <color=#3366CC>Black Sabbath</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Aerosmith</color>, <color=#3366CC>Alice Cooper</color>, Blue Öyster Cult, <color=#3366CC>Deep Purple</color>, <color=#3366CC>Queen</color>, <color=#3366CC>Van Halen</color>, <color=#3366CC>Journey</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kiss</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ronnie James Dio</color>, <color=#3366CC>Rush</color>
and <color=#3366CC>Judas Priest</color> reach a new generation of fans.
The 1980s were also known for song parodies becoming more mainstream, a trend led by parodic musician <color=#3366CC>"Weird Al"</color>
<color=#3366CC>Yankovic</color>. He was best known for his <color=#3366CC>Michael Jackson</color> parodies "Eat It" and "Fat" as well as other parodies like
"Another One Rides The Bus" (parody of "Another One Bites The Dust" by <color=#3366CC>Queen</color>).
By 1989, the <color=#3366CC>hip-hop</color> scene had evolved, gaining recognition and exhibiting a stronger influence on the music industry.
This time period is also considered part of the golden age of hip-hop. The <color=#3366CC>Beastie Boys</color>, <color=#3366CC>Public Enemy</color>, <color=#3366CC>Run-D.M.C.</color>,

Grandmaster Flash, the <color=#3366CC>Furious Five</color>, <color=#3366CC>N.W.A</color>, <color=#3366CC>LL Cool J</color>, <color=#3366CC>De La Soul</color>, <color=#3366CC>A Tribe Called Quest</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ice-T</color>, DJ Jazzy Jeff & The
Fresh Prince, Tone Lōc, Biz Markie, <color=#3366CC>The Sugar Hill Gang</color> and others experienced success in this genre.
<color=#3366CC>Country music</color> advanced into a new realm of popularity with youth appeal and record-breaking marks. Groundbreaking
artists such as <color=#3366CC>Alabama</color>, Hank Williams Jr., Reba McEntire, <color=#3366CC>George Strait</color>, Ricky Skaggs, Janie Fricke, The Judds, and
Randy Travis achieved multiple platinum and award status, foreshadowing the genre's popularity explosion in the
1990s. Country legends from past decades, such as <color=#3366CC>George Jones</color>, <color=#3366CC>Waylon Jennings</color>, <color=#3366CC>Willie Nelson</color>, Conway Twitty,
the Oak Ridge Boys, <color=#3366CC>Kenny Rogers</color>, <color=#3366CC>Dolly Parton</color>, <color=#3366CC>Merle Haggard</color>, Don Williams, Crystal Gayle, Ronnie Milsap,
Barbara Mandrell, and the Statler Brothers, also remained popular and continued to score hits throughout the decade.

The <color=#3366CC>techno</color> style of electronic dance music emerged in <color=#3366CC>Detroit</color>, <color=#3366CC>Michigan</color>, during the mid to late 1980s. The <color=#3366CC>house</color>
<color=#3366CC>music</color> style, another form of electronic dance music, emerged in <color=#3366CC>Chicago</color>, <color=#3366CC>Illinois</color>, in the early 1980s. It was initially
popularized in mid-1980s discothèques catering to the African-American, Latino and gay communities, first in Chicago,
then in New York City and Detroit. It eventually reached Europe before becoming infused in mainstream pop and dance
music worldwide.
Leading <color=#3366CC>punk rock</color> bands included <color=#3366CC>Black Flag</color>, <color=#3366CC>Minor Threat</color>, Suicidal Tendencies and Minutemen. Punk rock gave birth
to many subgenres like <color=#3366CC>hardcore</color>, which in turn gave birth to a few counterculture movements, most notably the Straight
Edge movement which began in the early 1980s. College rock caught on in the underground scene of the 1980s in a

nationwide movement with a distinct <color=#3366CC>D.I.Y</color> approach. Bands like the <color=#3366CC>Pixies</color>, <color=#3366CC>R.E.M.</color>, The Replacements, <color=#3366CC>Sonic Youth</color>,
XTC, <color=#3366CC>The Smiths</color>, Echo & the Bunnymen, The Stone Roses, The Jesus and Mary Chain etc. experienced success in
this genre. The 1980s also saw the birth of the <color=#3366CC>grunge</color> genre, with the arrival of such bands as Soundgarden and
<color=#3366CC>Nirvana</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Siouxsie and the Banshees</color> and Pigbag were post punk bands. <color=#3366CC>New Order</color> and <color=#3366CC>U2</color> had post punk origins.
Former <color=#3366CC>Beatle</color> <color=#3366CC>John Lennon</color> and <color=#3366CC>Yoko Ono</color> released their joint number 1 album Double Fantasy in November 1980.
This was Lennon's final album before his murder in December 1980. <color=#3366CC>Led Zeppelin</color> disbanded after drummer John
Bonham's 1980 death. Brian Johnson became lead singer of <color=#3366CC>AC/DC</color> after predecessor Bon Scott died in 1980. Reggae
musician <color=#3366CC>Bob Marley</color> died from a lentiginous skin <color=#3366CC>melanoma</color> in 1981. Motown singer <color=#3366CC>Marvin Gaye</color> was shot dead by his
father in 1984. Airplane crashes killed Ozzy Osbourne's guitarist Randy Rhoads in 1982, and <color=#3366CC>Kyu Sakamoto</color> in 1985.
Karen Carpenter died from complications of <color=#3366CC>anorexia nervosa</color> in 1983. Her death resulted in widespread attention and
research into eating disorders and body dysmorphia. Other deaths include Tim Hardin in 1980, Harry Chapin in 1981,
<color=#3366CC>Metallica</color> bassist Cliff Burton in 1986, Andy Gibb in 1988 and <color=#3366CC>Hibari Misora</color> in 1989.
In 1984, the British supergroup Band Aid was formed to raise aid and awareness of the economic plight of <color=#3366CC>Ethiopia</color>. In
1985's <color=#3366CC>Live Aid</color> concert, featuring many artists, promoted attention and action to send food aid to <color=#3366CC>Ethiopia</color> whose
people were suffering from a major <color=#3366CC>famine</color>.

The film industry
The 1980s saw the return of studio-driven films, coming from the filmmaker-driven <color=#3366CC>New Hollywood</color> era of the 1970s.
The period was when 'high concept' films gained popularity, where movies were to be easily marketable and
understandable, and, therefore, they had short cinematic <color=#3366CC>plots</color> that could be summarized in one or two sentences. The
modern Hollywood <color=#3366CC>blockbuster</color> is the most popular film format from the 1980s. Producer Don Simpson is usually
credited with the creation of the high-concept picture of the modern Hollywood blockbuster. In the mid-1980s, a wave of
British directors, including <color=#3366CC>Ridley Scott</color>, Alan Parker, Adrian Lyne and Tony Scott (with the latter directing a number of
Don Simpson films) ushered in a new era of blockbusters using the crowd-pleasing skills they had honed in UK
television commercials.
A significant development in the home media business is the establishment of The Criterion Collection in 1984, an
American company "dedicated to gathering the greatest films from around the world and publishing them in editions
that offer the highest technical quality". Through their releases, they were able to introduce what is now a standard to
home video: letterboxing to retain the original aspect ratio, film commentaries and supplements/special features.
Live-action films
The 1980s saw the golden age of teen films. Class, Fast Times at Ridgemont High, Risky Business, Mannequin,
Porky's, Valley Girl, and <color=#3366CC>John Hughes</color> directed or written Sixteen Candles, The Breakfast Club, Weird Science, Ferris
Bueller's Day Off, Pretty in Pink and Some Kind of Wonderful, were popular teen comedies, and their stars include
Emilio Estevez, Anthony Michael Hall, Jennifer Jason Leigh, Andrew McCarthy, Rob Lowe, Judd Nelson, Molly
Ringwald, Ally Sheedy, Matthew Broderick, <color=#3366CC>Tom Cruise</color>, Rebecca De Mornay, <color=#3366CC>Sean Penn</color> and <color=#3366CC>Nicolas Cage</color>. Other
youth dramas include Stand by Me and <color=#3366CC>Francis Ford Coppola</color> directed The Outsiders and Rumble Fish. Their stars
include River Phoenix and <color=#3366CC>Mickey Rourke</color>. The Brat Pack films are said to include The Breakfast Club and St. Elmo's
Fire. Musical dance films include Footloose, Dirty Dancing and Flashdance, and their stars include <color=#3366CC>Kevin Bacon</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Patrick Swayze</color>. Other musicals include Annie.
Horror films were a popular genre during the decade. Among the most popular horror franchises of the 1980s were the
Friday the 13th, A Nightmare on Elm Street, Halloween, Child's Play, Hellraiser, and Poltergeist franchises. Their casts
include <color=#3366CC>Jamie Lee Curtis</color>, <color=#3366CC>Robert Englund</color>, Catherine Hicks, Chris Sarandon and Brad Dourif. <color=#3366CC>The Shining</color> was initially
met with mixed reviews from critics, and even from the <color=#3366CC>author</color> of the book, and was moderately financially successful,
but later became very popular and critically acclaimed. The concept of the B horror film gave rise to many horror films
that went on to earn cult status, such as The Evil Dead, which was directed by Sam Raimi. Comedy horror films
included Beetlejuice, Gremlins, Little Shop of Horrors and The Lost Boys. Their stars include <color=#3366CC>Alec Baldwin</color>, <color=#3366CC>Geena</color>
<color=#3366CC>Davis</color>, <color=#3366CC>Winona Ryder</color>, Zach Galligan, Phoebe Cates, Corey Feldman, Corey Haim and <color=#3366CC>Kiefer Sutherland</color>.
Comedies included The Blues Brothers, Caddyshack, Stir Crazy, Private Benjamin, 9 to 5, Trading Places, Splash,
Jumpin' Jack Flash, Three Men and a Baby, Harry and the Hendersons, Throw Momma from the Train, Planes, Trains
and Automobiles, Twins, The 'Burbs and the original two Ghostbusters films, and their stars included <color=#3366CC>Dan Aykroyd</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Chevy Chase</color>, <color=#3366CC>Gene Wilder</color>, <color=#3366CC>Richard Pryor</color>, <color=#3366CC>Goldie Hawn</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jane Fonda</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tom Hanks</color>, <color=#3366CC>Whoopi Goldberg</color>, <color=#3366CC>Ted Danson</color>,

which starred the likes of Moranis, Candy, and <color=#3366CC>Leslie Nielsen</color>. Romcoms include Look Who's Talking, starring <color=#3366CC>John</color>
<color=#3366CC>Travolta</color>. Good Morning, Vietnam is a war comedy starring <color=#3366CC>Robin Williams</color> and Forest Whitaker. Action comedies
include 48 Hrs., Romancing the Stone and The Jewel of the Nile. Their stars include Nick Nolte and <color=#3366CC>Kathleen Turner</color>.

Animated films
After leaving <color=#3366CC>Disney</color> in 1979, <color=#3366CC>Don Bluth</color> formed his own studio and went on direct The Secret of NIMH, An American
Tail, The Land Before Time and All Dogs Go to Heaven. The Disney studio was almost bankrupted after The Black
Cauldron bombed at the box office. They began to recover with the modest success of Ron Clements and John Musker
directed The Great Mouse Detective. The live-action animated hybrid <color=#3366CC>Robert Zemeckis</color> directed <color=#3366CC>Who Framed Roger</color>
<color=#3366CC>Rabbit</color> co-produced with Steven Spielberg was successful, and the <color=#3366CC>Disney Renaissance</color> began with The Little
Mermaid, starring Jodi Benson.
Animated films based on popular works include Bon Voyage, Charlie Brown (and Don't Come Back!!), Heavy Metal,
The Adventures of Mark Twain, The Care Bears Movie, The Transformers: The Movie and The Chipmunk Adventure;
while original films include The Last Unicorn, The Plague Dogs, Rock & Rule, Fire and Ice, Abra Cadabra, The Brave
Little Toaster, The BFG, and the first Wallace & Gromit film, A Grand Day Out.
The 1980s also saw a surge of <color=#3366CC>Japanese anime films</color>: <color=#3366CC>Hayao Miyazaki</color>'s The Castle of Cagliostro and Nausicaä of the
Valley of the Wind were successful and led to the foundation of <color=#3366CC>Studio Ghibli</color>, which produced the successful Castle in
the Sky, <color=#3366CC>My Neighbor Totoro</color>, <color=#3366CC>Grave of the Fireflies</color> and Kiki's Delivery Service in the 1980s. Other well-known anime
films of that decade include Golgo 13: The Professional, Macross: Do You Remember Love?, Lensman, Vampire
Hunter D, <color=#3366CC>Akira</color>, Little Nemo: Adventures in Slumberland and the Urusei Yatsura film series. The first theatrical
animated franchise, the Doraemon film series began in 1980 with the release of Doraemon: Nobita's Dinosaur.
Television
Music video channel <color=#3366CC>MTV</color> was launched in the United States in 1981 and had a profound impact on the <color=#3366CC>music industry</color>
and <color=#3366CC>popular culture</color>, especially in the 1980s and early 1990s.
The 1980s was a decade of transformation in television. <color=#3366CC>Cable television</color> became more accessible and therefore, more
popular. By the middle of the decade, almost 70% of the US population had cable television and over 85% were paying
for cable services such as <color=#3366CC>HBO</color> or Showtime. People who lived in rural areas where cable TV service was not available
could still access cable channels through a large (and expensive) satellite dish, which, by the mid-1990s, was phased
out in favor of the small rooftop dishes that offer DirecTV and Dish Network services.
<color=#3366CC>CNN</color> and Bravo began in 1980; Channel 4, Rete 4 and Italia 1 in 1982; RTL and Canal+ in 1984; <color=#3366CC>Fox</color> in 1986; M6 in
1987; Turner Network Television in 1988; CNBC and ProSieben in 1989.
New prime-time <color=#3366CC>soap operas</color> included <color=#3366CC>Dallas</color>, its spin-off Knots Landing, Dynasty, Falcon Crest, <color=#3366CC>EastEnders</color> and
